344.title: The price of calm
344.hook: spilled oil, stolen wine: say, this is what peace of mind costs (Enchiridion 12)
344.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat small losses and annoyances as the price of tranquility, naming the cost and letting it go rather than stewing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Job, and the trade of verbs: not I lost it, but I gave it back. Your line was care for it like an inn.

Somebody at work ate your yogurt from the office fridge. Your name was on it. In marker. You could spend the afternoon on this: draft the passive-aggressive note, investigate, tell three people. Or you could do some quick math. The yogurt cost about a dollar. The afternoon of stewing costs a lot more. Epictetus did this math with olive oil and wine. Section twelve of the handbook puts a price tag on peace of mind, and the surprise is how cheap it is.
screen: `THE STOLEN YOGURT.` → `THE AFTERNOON OF STEWING.` → `A PRICE TAG ON PEACE.`

segments.voice: If you want to make progress, Epictetus says, drop thoughts like: if I don't watch my affairs, I'll have nothing to live on. Better, he says bluntly, to die of hunger free of grief and fear than to live in plenty and be troubled. That's strong, and he means it as a direction, not a test. Then the kitchen. Begin with small things, he says. A little oil spilled. A little wine stolen. Say to yourself: this is the price of tranquility, the price of being undisturbed. Nothing is had for nothing. Tranquility here translates ataraxia: a, not, and a root meaning stirred up. Unstirred, like a pond on a still morning. Then the servant, and an honest note. Epictetus finishes with a household scene: you call your servant and he may not come, or may come and do the wrong thing. He isn't so important, Epictetus says, that it's in his power to disturb you. Epictetus' examples come from a world where owning people was ordinary, and he had been enslaved himself. That's worth noticing plainly, and the point that travels still stands: other people's choices aren't a lever on your calm unless you hand it to them. So the yogurt. A dollar. That's the price, and paid gladly, it buys an afternoon back. Small days, small prices. The expensive part is refusing to pay.

segments.voice: Pick up something small within reach, a coin, a pen, a paper clip, and let it stand for one annoyance from today or yesterday: a spill, a late delivery, a parking ticket, the yogurt. Hold it in your palm and name its price, out loud or inside: this is what calm costs. Then set it down, the way you'd put coins on a counter, and sit with what you bought.
Ataraxia, tranquility, the state of staying undisturbed: a little spilled oil, a little stolen wine, the small price of calm. Nothing is had for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: nothing is had for nothing. Calm has a price, and it's usually small. Day three hundred forty-four.

345.title: Content to seem foolish
345.hook: if you want to improve, be willing to look foolish about outside things (Enchiridion 13)
345.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners deliberately accept looking uninformed or unfashionable about outside matters, as training in caring less about others' opinions.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ataraxia, the calm of staying unstirred. Your line was nothing is had for nothing.

Athens. A merchant named Zeno, recently shipwrecked, has found a teacher: Crates the Cynic. One day, as Diogenes Laertius tells it, Crates hands him a pot of lentil soup to carry through the busy potters' quarter. Zeno tries to hide the pot under his cloak, embarrassed. Crates cracks it with his staff, and soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno bolts. Crates calls after him, roughly: why run away, little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Zeno would go on to found the Stoic school.
screen: `ZENO AND A POT OF SOUP.` → `CRATES CRACKS IT.` → `NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: Section thirteen of the handbook says: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought foolish and simple about outside things. Not foolish about everything. About the outside things: the latest phone, the right restaurant, the gossip, who's up and who's down. Then the harder half. Don't wish to be thought to know anything, Epictetus says. And if people start to think you're somebody, be suspicious of yourself. That's a striking line from a famous teacher. It sounds like Socrates in Plato's Apology, who says he is wiser only in not thinking he knows what he doesn't. The reason: it isn't easy, he says, to keep your purpose in line with nature and also keep up with all the outside things. Care for one, and you're bound to neglect the other. Attention is limited. Spend it on looking clever and there's less left for being good. And it's training. Looking foolish can feel like a small death: the red face, the wish to explain. That's exactly what Crates' soup pot was training. Each time you survive it, you learn what Crates shouted: nothing terrible has happened. You asked the obvious question in the meeting, and the meeting went on. You wore last year's coat, and the sun came up. You said I don't know, and someone finally explained it. People may think you're a little behind. Let them think it. Your attention stays free for what's really yours.

Your line: let them think it. A red face passes, and the meeting goes on. Day three hundred forty-five, done.

346.title: Who holds the leash
346.hook: whoever controls what you want is your master (Enchiridion 14)
346.carry: the slack shows up at this end
346.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism notice which wants make them dependent on others, such as approval or replies, and practice wanting them less urgently.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Crates, who cracked Zeno's soup pot. Your line was let them think it.

A phone buzzes on a table. Three people at dinner glance at it, including the person who swore they weren't going to. Somewhere, someone who designed that buzz is very pleased. Here's a strange way to measure freedom: not by what you're allowed to do, but by how many hands can tug you. If anyone who can give or withhold what you badly want can move you, they have a kind of leash on you. Epictetus spent his youth legally owned by another man. He knew what a master was.
screen: `THE PHONE BUZZES.` → `HOW MANY HANDS CAN TUG YOU?` → `WHO HOLDS THE LEASH.`

segments.voice: Section fourteen of the handbook opens bluntly. If you want your children and your partner and your friends to live forever, Epictetus says, you're being foolish: you want things that aren't up to you to be up to you. If you want other people never to make mistakes, same problem. He isn't saying don't love them. He's saying don't demand what no one can promise. Then the definition. Each person's master, he says, is whoever has the power to give or take away what that person wants or wants to avoid. That's the leash. Not chains. Wanting. So whoever wants to be free, he says, should neither want nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, that person is bound to be a slave. It's a severe word, and he chose it knowing exactly what it meant. Now look at what tugs a modern day: a boss's approval, a crush's reply, likes on a post, a parent's praise, a number on a scale. None of those people or things are bad. But each time peace depends on them, someone is handed the end of a leash, often without asking for it. Epictetus' point is that a lot of these leashes can be let go of from your end. You can still want the reply. You can just stop needing it. The person holding the other end may never notice. The slack shows up at this end.

segments.voice: Picture your day as a field with a few leashes trailing from you, to a phone, a person's opinion, a number, and follow one to whoever holds the other end. Ask what you want from them that they can give or withhold. Don't cut it; just loosen your own grip a little, and feel the slack.
Epictetus, once legally owned himself, measures freedom by who controls what you want or fear, until you let that want go. Today's word.

347.title: Life as a banquet
347.hook: when a dish reaches you, take a modest share; if it passes, don't reach after it (Enchiridion 15)
347.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat good things as dishes passed at a banquet: they take a moderate share when one arrives, and try not to grasp ahead or hold on as it passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epictetus, and who holds the leash. Your line was the slack shows up at this end.
screen: `THE SLACK SHOWS UP AT THIS END.`

segments.voice: A big family dinner. The bowls go around the table, left to right. Mashed potatoes, the good rolls, the one dish everyone fights over. You can see it coming, four people away. An uncle has already half stood up to reach for it. A cousin watches it with her fork raised. And one person, usually an older aunt, just talks to whoever's beside her, takes a spoonful when the bowl arrives, and passes it on. Epictetus would have liked that aunt. Section fifteen of the handbook is set at exactly this kind of table.
screen: `BOWLS GOING AROUND THE TABLE.` → `THE UNCLE HALF STANDING.` → `THE AUNT WHO JUST PASSES IT ON.`

segments.voice: Remember, Epictetus says, to behave in life as at a banquet. A dish is carried around and reaches you: put out your hand and take a modest share. It passes you by: don't hold it back. It hasn't come yet: don't send your desire out ahead to meet it. Wait until it's in front of you. That last one is subtle. A lot of grabbing happens before anything arrives, in the head: at the promotion not yet offered, the house not yet seen, the relationship already being planned. Do the same, he says, with children, with a spouse, with office, with wealth. They come around. They pass. Take your share well when they reach you, and you'll be a worthy guest at the banquet of the gods. He adds a further step, for a few: if you can let some dishes go by even when they're offered, you'll share not just the gods' table but their rule. He names Diogenes the Cynic and Heraclitus as people who lived that way. Banquet here is symposion, a drinking together, the same word as Plato's dialogue. Ancient dinners had customs about how the dishes and the cup moved, and Epictetus turns manners everyone knew into a whole philosophy of having. Good things come around. Take a fair share. Pass it on. Don't lean down the table after the next bowl.
screen: `A DISH REACHES YOU: A MODEST SHARE.` · `PASSED: DON'T HOLD IT. NOT YET: WAIT.` · `CHILDREN, OFFICE, WEALTH, ON THE DISHES.` · `SYMPOSION: DRINKING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `WHEN THE DISH COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're reaching ahead for, something that hasn't come to your end of the table yet: a trip, a result, a bit of good news. Notice your hand, as it were, already stretched toward it, and gently bring it back to your lap. Then look at what's in front of you right now, this breath, this chair, this moment, and take a modest share of it.
Symposion, the Greek word for banquet: take a modest share when the dish reaches you, let it pass, and don't reach ahead. Today's word.
Your line: when the dish comes. What's in front of you is your share for now. That's day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: Beside the weeping
348.hook: sit with a grieving friend and sigh with them, but don't groan inside; some readers find this cool, others wise (Enchiridion 16)
348.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism comfort the grieving with real warmth in word and gesture while trying to stay inwardly steady, so they can keep showing up.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was symposion, life as a banquet. Your line was when the dish comes.

Lifeguards learn a hard rule early. When someone is drowning, you don't just leap in and grab them. A panicking swimmer can pull the rescuer under, and then there are two people in trouble instead of one. You go in with a float, you stay on top of the water, and from there you can actually help. Grief can work like deep water. A friend calls, sobbing, and it's easy to dive straight in, until you're crying too hard to hear what they need. Section sixteen of the handbook is about exactly this moment.
screen: `THE LIFEGUARD'S RULE.` → `TWO IN THE WATER.` → `BESIDE THE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: When you see someone weeping in grief, Epictetus says, because a child has gone far away, or because they've lost their property, don't let the impression carry you off, as if they were truly in the grip of an outside evil. Have ready, he says, the thought: it isn't the event itself that crushes this person, since someone else meets the same event and isn't crushed. It's their judgment about it. That's day three hundred thirty-seven, dogma, turned toward someone else. And yet, he says, don't hesitate to sympathize with them in words, and even, if the moment calls for it, to sigh and groan along with them. Only take care not to groan inwardly as well. Sit with them. Speak gently. Just don't drown. Some people find this passage cool, even a little false: comforting someone while privately thinking their grief is a mistake. Others find it wise and practical, the lifeguard's float: you stay steady enough to stay present, to bring soup on day fifteen, to call again in a month. Epictetus himself doesn't tell you to say the inner sentence out loud. That would be cruel, and nothing in the text suggests it. Neighbors have their own words for the outward part. Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James words: "weep with them that weep." Epictetus pairs that outward part with a steady one inside.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who is hurting right now, and picture sitting beside them, your face soft, real sympathy coming the way it would. Then, underneath, find your own feet: the floor, your breath going in and out, steady. Warmth on the outside, ground on the inside, both at once.
Paul, who wrote weep with them that weep: sigh with a grieving friend, sympathize in words, but keep steady inside, so you can stay. Today's word.
Your line: with them, steady. Your warmth helps most when your feet stay on the floor. See you tomorrow.

349.title: An actor in a play
349.hook: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote; your job is to play the part well (Enchiridion 17)
349.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism think of their circumstances as a role they didn't choose, and put their effort into playing it well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paul, who wrote weep with them that weep. Your line was with them, steady.

The school play is cast, and a kid who wanted the lead is the third tree from the left. One version of that kid sulks through every rehearsal. Another decides to be the best third tree the school has ever seen: swaying in the wind on cue, rustling at the sad part. The parents in the audience notice that tree. Nobody chose their role, and the play didn't care. What they did with it was theirs. Epictetus took the theater and made it a picture of a life.
screen: `THE THIRD TREE FROM THE LEFT.` → `SULK, OR SWAY ON CUE.` → `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY.`

segments.voice: Remember, Epictetus says in section seventeen, that you are an actor in a play, and the play is as the author wants it. If short, then short. If long, then long. If the author wants you to play a poor man, play even that one well. Or someone lame, or an official, or a private citizen. He lists them flatly, beggar and governor side by side, as if they were just costumes. Then the line that splits the work. Your business, he says, is to play the given part well. Choosing the part belongs to another. Who is the author? The section doesn't say. Elsewhere Epictetus speaks of God or Zeus; some modern readers hear nature, or circumstance, or simply the hand you were dealt. Either way, the split is the same. Casting isn't yours. Acting is. The Greek for actor was hypokrites. English took it over and it slid into hypocrite: someone acting a part that isn't true. Epictetus means the opposite. Play your part truly, with your whole self. Centuries later Shakespeare wrote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players". Epictetus puts the weight elsewhere: merely, maybe, but the playing is everything you get to do. Parent, patient, new hire, caregiver, the one who stayed home this year. If someone hands you the third tree, sway like you mean it.

350.title: The raven croaks
350.hook: when a raven croaks an omen, remember no sign has power over your will (Enchiridion 18)
350.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet a bad omen or ominous news by reminding themselves that it concerns outer things, not their own choices, and asking what good they can draw from what comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hypokrites, the Greek for actor. Your line was play the part well.

A raven calls from a rooftop just as someone sets out on a journey. In Epictetus' world, that harsh croak could be read as a warning, an omen about the trip ahead. The handbook gives that moment a whole section. Modern life has its own versions. The text that just says, we need to talk. The dream that leaves a bad taste all morning. The black cat, the broken mirror, the gloomy forecast for the big day. Something small shows up, and it feels like a message about everything.
screen: `A RAVEN ON THE ROOF.` → `WE NEED TO TALK.` → `THE RAVEN CROAKS.`

segments.voice: When a raven croaks an unlucky omen, Epictetus says in section eighteen, don't let the impression carry you away. Instead, divide it at once, and say to yourself: none of this is a sign for me. It may be a sign about my poor body, or my property, or my reputation, or my children or my wife. But not about me, the part that chooses. Notice he doesn't say omens are nonsense. Elsewhere in the handbook he treats consulting a diviner as something people did, with its own proper limits, and that comes up in a couple of weeks. His point is narrower: whatever a sign might mean for the things outside you, it can't reach your will. Then the surprising turn. For me, he says, every sign is a good one, if I want it to be. Whatever comes of it, it's up to me to draw some benefit from it. A bad harvest, a lost case, a scandal: each one is material for patience or courage or honesty. The raven can croak whatever it likes. And the modern ravens? The text that says we need to talk often just means a talk. The bad dream was a dream. Even when the sign is right and trouble comes, the sorting still holds: it touches the outer pile, not the inner one. A look back at the week: ataraxia, Crates, the leash, the banquet, Paul beside the weeping, the actor, and today the raven. Seven ways of keeping the inner pile your own.
screen: `DON'T BE CARRIED AWAY.` · `NO SIGN FOR ME, ONLY MY OUTER THINGS.` · `EVERY SIGN IS GOOD, IF I WISH.` · `OUR RAVENS.` · then, large: `JUST A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one bad omen from this week, a message, a dream, a feeling about tomorrow, and let it croak once in your mind. Sort it the way Epictetus does: this might be about my plans, my money, my reputation, not about me, the one who chooses. Then ask what you could make of it, whatever comes, and let the bird fly off.
Omen. Epictetus' answer to a bad sign: it may point at your outer things, never at your will, and whatever comes, you can draw good from it. Today's word.
Your line: just a bird. A week of keeping the inner pile, done. That's day three hundred fifty.
